'''暦博士'''（れきはかせ）は、[[日本]]の[[律令制]]における[[官職]]の1つ。[[中務省]][[陰陽寮]]に属して、毎年の造暦（[[暦]]の作成）と[[改暦]]、[[日食]]の予測、[[暦生]]の教育にあたった。定員1名（後に[[権官]]1名追加）・[[従七位上]]相当（ただし、後世では[[五位]]以上が慣例となる）。[[和訓]]は「こよみのはかせ」。[[唐名]]は司暦・司暦正保。
『[[日本書紀]]』においては、[[欽明天皇]]14年条に登場するのが最古であるが、実際の官制整備は後代のことである。[[延暦]]10年（[[791年]]）に[[職田]]3町が設定される。古くは[[暦道]]・[[算道]]に通じた[[渡来人]]系の人物が任じられる事が多かったが、後に[[大春日氏]]・[[家原氏]]・[[大中臣氏]]・[[賀茂氏]]などが[[世襲]]した。[[清和天皇]]の頃に[[五紀暦]]・[[宣明暦]]の導入を主唱した[[大春日真野麻呂]]や[[大衍暦]]を日本に持ち帰った[[吉備真備]]の6代目の子孫とされる[[賀茂忠行]]が良く知られた。忠行の子・[[賀茂保憲]]は暦博士と[[天文博士]]を兼ねたが、その死後は保憲の子・[[賀茂光栄]]の子孫が暦道を、門人[[安倍晴明]]の子孫が[[天文道]]を継承した。
後に賀茂家の嫡流が断絶すると、同氏の庶流であった[[幸徳井友景]]が[[陰陽頭]]となり、孫の[[幸徳井友傳|友傳]]以後は[[幸徳井家]]の世襲となる。だが、[[陰陽道]]においては[[土御門家_(安倍氏)|土御門家]]が、[[暦学]]においては[[江戸幕府|幕府]][[天文方]]が圧迫を加えたために、後世の幸徳井家は専ら[[暦注]]のみを担当するにとどまった。[[明治維新]]後の陰陽寮の廃止とともに暦博士も廃止され、間もなく[[太陽暦]]への改暦によってその役目は終わる事になる。

'''暦博士'''（れきはかせ）は、[[日本]]の[[律令制]]における[[官職]]の1つ。[[中務省]][[陰陽寮]]に属して、毎年の造暦（[[暦]]の作成）と[[改暦]]、[[日食]]の予測、[[暦生]]の教育にあたった。定員1名（後に[[権官]]1名追加）・[[従七位上]]相当（ただし、後世では[[五位]]以上が慣例となる）。[[和訓]]は「こよみのはかせ」。[[唐名]]は司暦・司暦正保。
== 概要 == 『[[日本書紀]]』においては、[[欽明天皇]]14年（[[553年]]）条に登場するのが最古である。同年、6月に百済に暦博士を[[番]]によって日本に派遣することを求めている。これは当時、新羅との軍事的緊張下にあった百済に対する日本の軍事的支援に対する見返りであったと考えられ、日本からの継続的支援を希望する百済が暦博士を派遣しても毎年の暦の作成・提供に留まり、[[暦学]]伝授には応じなかったとする見方がある<ref>鎌田元一「暦と時間」（初出:上原真人 他編『列島の古代史 ひと・もの・こと』第7巻（岩波書店、2006年）/所収:鎌田『律令国家史の研究』（塙書房、2008年））</ref>。そのため、実際の官制整備は、[[観勒]]が暦学を伝えた後の後代のことである。[[延暦]]10年（[[791年]]）に[[職田]]3町が設定される。古くは[[暦道]]・[[算道]]に通じた[[渡来人]]系の人物が任じられる事が多かったが、後に[[大春日氏]]・[[家原氏]]・[[大中臣氏]]・[[賀茂氏]]などが[[世襲]]した。[[清和天皇]]の頃に[[五紀暦]]・[[宣明暦]]の導入を主唱した[[大春日真野麻呂]]や[[大衍暦]]を日本に持ち帰った[[吉備真備]]の6代目の子孫とされる[[賀茂忠行]]が良く知られた。忠行の子・[[賀茂保憲]]は暦博士と[[天文博士]]を兼ねたが、その死後は保憲の子・[[賀茂光栄]]の子孫が暦道を、門人[[安倍晴明]]の子孫が[[天文道]]を継承した。なお、暦書を私的に持つことは[[雑令]]の秘書玄象令で厳しく規制されたために朝廷外に人材を求めるのは困難であり、[[平将門]]が「新皇」を名乗って文武百官を任じた際も暦博士は任命できず、同様に[[吉野朝廷]]（[[南朝 (日本)|南朝]]）も暦博士を置けなかったらしく、その元号が入った[[具注暦]]は存在しない。
後に賀茂家の嫡流が断絶すると、同氏の庶流であった[[幸徳井友景]]が[[陰陽頭]]となり、孫の[[幸徳井友傳|友傳]]以後は暦博士の官職は[[幸徳井家]]の世襲となる。だが、[[陰陽道]]においては[[土御門家_(安倍氏)|土御門家]]が、[[暦学]]においては[[江戸幕府|幕府]][[天文方]]が圧迫を加えたために、後世の幸徳井家は専ら[[暦注]]のみを担当するにとどまった。[[明治維新]]後の陰陽寮の廃止とともに暦博士も廃止され、間もなく[[太陽暦]]への改暦によってその役目は終わる事になる。
== 脚注 == <references />

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
==In media== === Books === * ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Aramata]], published in 1985 * ''[[Onmyōji (novel series)|Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Baku Yumemakura]], published in 1988 * ''[[The Summer of the Ubume]]'', ''[[Mōryō no Hako]]'' and other Kyōgokudō series, written by [[Natsuhiko Kyogoku]], published in 1994 * ''{{ill|Onmyō no Miyako|ja|陰陽ノ京}}'', written by [[Soichiro Watase]], published in 2001 * ''[[Shōnen Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Mitsuru Yūki]], published in 2001 * ''[[Rental Magica]]'', written by {{ill|Makoto Sanda|ja|三田誠}}, published in 2004 * ''{{ill|Bakemonogatari|ja|化物語}}'', written by [[Nisio Isin]], published in 2005 * ''[[Fairy Navigator Runa]]'', written by {{ill|Miyoko Ikeda|ja|池田美代子}}, published in 2008 * ''[[Tokyo Ravens]]'', written by {{ill|Kōhei Azano|ja|あざの耕平}}, published in 2010
=== Manga and anime ===
* ''[[Tokyo Babylon]]'', written by [[Clamp (manga artists)|Clamp]], published in 1990 * ''[[X (manga)|X]]'', written by Clamp, published in 1992 * ''[[Shaman King]]'', written by [[Hiroyuki Takei]], published in 1998 * ''[[Gag Manga Biyori]]'', written by [[Kōsuke Masuda]], published in 2000 * ''[[Magical Shopping Arcade Abenobashi]]'', created by [[Gainax]], published in 2001 * ''[[Amatsuki]]'', written by {{ill|Shinobu Takayama|ja|高山しのぶ}}, published in 2002 * ''[[Gin Tama]]'', written by [[Hideaki Sorachi]], published in 2003 * ''[[xxxHolic]]'', written by Clamp, published in 2003 * ''[[Onmyō Taisenki]]'', written by Yoshihiko Tomizawa, published in 2003 * ''[[Musashi Gundoh]]'', based on an unused story by [[Monkey Punch]], published in 2006 * ''{{ill|Shibariya Komachi|ja|縛り屋小町}}'', written by [[Mick Takeuchi]], published in 2006 * ''[[Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Shiibashi]], published in 2008 * ''[[Twin Star Exorcists]]'', written by {{ill|Yoshiaki Sukeno|ja|助野嘉昭}}, published in 2013 * ''[[The Reincarnation of the Strongest Exorcist in Another World |The Reincarnation of the Strongest Exorcist in Another World]]'', written by Kiichi Kosuzu, published in 2018 * ''[[MAO (manga)|MAO]]'', written by [[Rumiko Takahashi]], published in 2019
=== Films === *''[[Tokyo: The Last Megalopolis]]'', a 1988 Japanese fantasy film directed by [[Akio Jissōji]], based on the novel ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'' by Hiroshi Aramata *[[Onmyōji (film)|''Onmyōji'' (film)]], a 2001 Japanese film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura and released in the U.S. in 2003 as ''Onmyōji - The Yin Yang Master'' **''[[Onmyōji 2]]'', the 2003 sequel *''[[The Yin-Yang Master: Dream of Eternity]]'', a 2020 Chinese fantasy film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura directed by [[Guo Jingming]], and starring [[Mark Chao]] and [[Deng Lun]] *''[[The Yinyang Master]]'', a 2021 Chinese fantasy film directed by Li Weiran, and starring [[Chen Kun]], [[Zhou Xun]] and [[William Chan]] based on the game that was based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura
=== Video games === * ''{{ill|Kuon no Kizuna|ja|久遠の絆}}'', developed by [[FOG Inc.]], released in 1998 * ''[[Tokyo Majin Gakuen]]'', produced by {{ill|Shūhō Imai|ja|今井秋芳}}, released in 1998 * ''[[Kuon]]'', developed by [[FromSoftware]], released in 2004 * ''[[11eyes: Tsumi to Batsu to Aganai no Shōjo]]'', developed by {{ill|Lass (video game developer)|lt=Lass|ja|Lass}}, released in 2008 * ''[[Naraka: Bladepoint]]'', developed by [[24 Entertainment]], released in 2021 features the character [[Kurumi Tsuchimikado]], who according to game lore is the first female Onmyōji, descended from a long line of Onmyōdō masters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.narakathegame.com/index.html|title = Naraka: Bladepoint - New Hero Out Now!}}</ref>

{{draft}}
{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}}
{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}}
{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.
