He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. '''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=original at [[every:Reki Hakase]][[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:23, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to __NOINDEX__ [[Onmyodo]] [[ja:暦博士]] Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|平将門}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.
