__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.

This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.

This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. __NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|清和天皇}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."

This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). __NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.
