__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

__NOINDEX__ [[ja:暦博士]]
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦}}.

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|12=draft}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|12=draft}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|12=draft}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|12=draft}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

__NOINDEX__ '''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|12=draft}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|12=draft}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

__NOINDEX__ '''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|12=draft}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|12=draft}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

__NOINDEX__ '''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|12=draft}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|12=draft}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

__NOINDEX__ '''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|12=draft}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[Ministry of Central Affairs|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|1=Yin-Yang Bureau|2=ja|3=陰陽寮|4=fr|5=Bureau d'Onmyō|6=zh|7=阴阳寮|8=ko|9=음양료|12=draft}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ({{ill|暦|ja|暦|12=draft}}), revisions ({{ill|改暦|ja|改暦|1=Calendar reform|12=draft}}), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|12=draft}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|12=draft}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|12=draft}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."
== Overview == The earliest mention of the position appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor {{ill|Kinmei|ja|欽明天皇|12=draft}}'s reign (553) for the kingdom of {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|12=draft}} to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅|12=draft}}, likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|12=draft}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like {{ill|Kanroku|ja|観勒|12=draft}}.
In {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦|12=draft}} 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often {{ill|渡来人|ja|渡来人|12=draft}} families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|12=draft}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|ja|算道|12=draft}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|12=draft}} became hereditary holders.
Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=draft}}, who advocated for adopting the {{ill|Goki Calendar|ja|五紀暦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Senmyō Calendar|ja|宣明暦|12=draft}} during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=draft}}'s reign, and {{ill|Kibi no Makibi|ja|吉備真備|12=draft}}, credited with introducing the {{ill|Dai'en Calendar|ja|大衍暦|12=draft}} to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=draft}} and his son, {{ill|Kamo no Yasunori|ja|賀茂保憲|12=draft}}, were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student {{ill|Abe no Seimei|ja|安倍晴明|12=draft}}'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=draft}} tradition.
Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=draft}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=draft}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代|12=draft}}, neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.
When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=draft}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=draft}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=draft}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft}} in {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Bakufu Tenmonkata|ja|天文方|12=draft}} in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=draft}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the {{ill|Gregorian calendar|ja|太陽暦|12=draft}}.

The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Tadayuki|qq=}} and his son, [[:en:Kamo no Yasunori|Kamo no Yasunori]], were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student [[:en:Abe no Seimei|Abe no Seimei]]'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/天文道|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmondō (astrology)|qq=}} tradition.

Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} in [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] and the [[:en:Tenmongata|Bakufu Tenmonkata]] in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. __NOINDEX__
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦博士|13=User:Immanuelle/Reki Hakase|qq=}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[:en:Ministry of the Center|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|1=Yin-Yang Bureau|2=ja|3=陰陽寮|4=fr|5=Bureau d'Onmyō|6=zh|7=阴阳寮|8=ko|9=음양료|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōryō|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Bureau|qq=}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ([[:en:Calendar|暦]]), revisions ([[:en:Calendar reform|Calendar reform]]), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦生|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a Rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Seventh Rank|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 従七位}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held Ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fifth Rank|qq=|1=Five Ranks|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q903222}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."

== Overview ==
The earliest mention of the position appears in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kinmei|Kinmei]]'s reign (553) for the kingdom of [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with [[:en:Silla|Silla]], likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦学|qq=|1=rekigaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514951}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like [[:en:Gwalleuk|Kanroku]].

In [[:en:Enryaku|Enryaku]] 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharu no Ason|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ie-no-Miyako clan|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōnakatomi clan|qq=}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Asomi clan|qq=|1=Kamo no Ason clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q122979457}} became hereditary holders.

{{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Reki Hakase|13=User:Immanuelle/Reki Hakase|qq=}} is a topic related to   [[:en:Onmyodo|Onmyodo]]

__NOINDEX__
'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦博士|13=User:Immanuelle/Reki Hakase|qq=}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[:en:Ministry of the Center|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|1=Yin-Yang Bureau|2=ja|3=陰陽寮|4=fr|5=Bureau d'Onmyō|6=zh|7=阴阳寮|8=ko|9=음양료|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōryō|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Bureau|qq=}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ([[:en:Calendar|暦]]), revisions ([[:en:Calendar reform|Calendar reform]]), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦生|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a Rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Seventh Rank|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 従七位}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held Ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fifth Rank|1=Five Ranks|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q903222}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."

== Overview ==
The earliest mention of the position appears in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kinmei|Kinmei]]'s reign (553) for the kingdom of [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with [[:en:Silla|Silla]], likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦学|1=rekigaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514951}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like [[:en:Gwalleuk|Kanroku]].

In [[:en:Enryaku|Enryaku]] 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often [[:en:Toraijin|渡来人]] families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦道|13=User:Immanuelle/Rekidō|qq=}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|1=Sandō_(mathematics)|2=ja|3=算道|lt=Sandō|ja|算道|1=Sandō_(mathematics)|2=ja|3=算道|lt=Sandō|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/算道|13=User:Immanuelle/Sandō_(mathematics)|qq=}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharu no Ason|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōnakatomi clan|qq=}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Asomi clan|1=Kamo no Ason clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q122979457}} became hereditary holders.

Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharu Manomaro|1=Ōharu Manomaro|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q27920625}}, who advocated for adopting the [[:en:Goki calendar|Goki Calendar]] and [[:en:Xuanming calendar|Senmyō Calendar]] during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiwa|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'s reign, and [[:en:Kibi no Makibi|Kibi no Makibi]], credited with introducing the [[:en:Taien calendar|Dai'en Calendar]] to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Tadayuki|qq=}} and his son, [[:en:Kamo no Yasunori|Kamo no Yasunori]], were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student [[:en:Abe no Seimei|Abe no Seimei]]'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/天文道|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmondō (astrology)|qq=}} tradition.

Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/雑令|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Masakado|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Masakado|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Southern Court (Japan)|1=Southern Dynasties|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1206988}} during the [[:en:Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|Nanboku-chō period]], neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.

When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui Family|lt=Kōtokui Family|lt=Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui clan|qq=}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui Tomokage|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} in [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] and the [[:en:Tenmongata|Bakufu Tenmonkata]] in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦注|1=rekichū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514953}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the [[:en:Solar calendar|Solar calendar]].

'''Reki Hakase''' ({{ill|暦博士|ja|暦博士|1=Reki Hakase|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦博士|13=User:Immanuelle/Reki Hakase|qq=}}) was a position within Japan's [[Ritsuryō system]], under the [[:en:Ministry of the Center|Nakatsukasashō]] and its {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮|1=Yin-Yang Bureau|2=ja|3=陰陽寮|4=fr|5=Bureau d'Onmyō|6=zh|7=阴阳寮|8=ko|9=음양료|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onmyōryō|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Bureau|qq=}} bureau. The role involved the annual creation of calendars ([[:en:Calendar|暦]]), revisions ([[:en:Calendar reform|Calendar reform]]), solar eclipse predictions, and education of calendrical students ({{ill|暦生|ja|暦生|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦生|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). The position was originally limited to one official (later expanded with an additional adjunct), with a Rank equivalent to {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|ja|従七位上|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Seventh Rank, Upper Grade|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Seventh Rank|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 従七位}}. Over time, holders of the position typically held Ranks of {{ill|Fifth Rank|ja|五位|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fifth Rank|1=Five Ranks|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q903222}} or higher. The position's traditional Japanese reading is "Koyomi no Hakase," and the Tang Chinese name was "Saireki" or "Saireki Seihō."

== Overview ==
The earliest mention of the position appears in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], which records a request in the 14th year of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kinmei|Kinmei]]'s reign (553) for the kingdom of [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] to send calendrical specialists to Japan. This request, made during heightened military tensions with [[:en:Silla|Silla]], likely reflected a quid pro quo for Japan's military aid to Baekje. Scholars suggest that Baekje preferred only to provide annual calendars rather than train Japanese officials in calendrical science ({{ill|暦学|ja|暦学|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦学|1=rekigaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514951}}). This reliance delayed the institutional establishment of the position until later periods, following the transmission of calendrical knowledge by figures like [[:en:Gwalleuk|Kanroku]].

In [[:en:Enryaku|Enryaku]] 10 (791), the office received an allotment of three ''shō'' (units) of rice fields for its operation. Early holders of the post were often [[:en:Toraijin|渡来人]] families versed in {{ill|暦道|ja|暦道|1=Rekidō|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦道|13=User:Immanuelle/Rekidō|qq=}} (calendrical studies) and {{ill|算道|1=Sandō_(mathematics)|2=ja|3=算道|lt=Sandō|ja|算道|1=Sandō_(mathematics)|2=ja|3=算道|lt=Sandō|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/算道|13=User:Immanuelle/Sandō_(mathematics)|qq=}} (mathematical studies). Over time, native Japanese families such as the {{ill|Ōharu no Ason|ja|大春日氏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharu no Ason|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja|家原氏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ie-no-Miyako clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōnakatomi clan|qq=}}, and {{ill|Kamo no Asomi clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Asomi clan|1=Kamo no Ason clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q122979457}} became hereditary holders.

Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharu Manomaro|1=Ōharu Manomaro|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q27920625}}, who advocated for adopting the [[:en:Goki calendar|Goki Calendar]] and [[:en:Xuanming calendar|Senmyō Calendar]] during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiwa|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'s reign, and [[:en:Kibi no Makibi|Kibi no Makibi]], credited with introducing the [[:en:Taien calendar|Dai'en Calendar]] to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Tadayuki|qq=}} and his son, [[:en:Kamo no Yasunori|Kamo no Yasunori]], were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student [[:en:Abe no Seimei|Abe no Seimei]]'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/天文道|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmondō (astrology)|qq=}} tradition.

Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/雑令|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Masakado|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Masakado|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Southern Court (Japan)|1=Southern Dynasties|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1206988}} during the [[:en:Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|Nanboku-chō period]], neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.

When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui Family|lt=Kōtokui Family|lt=Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui clan|qq=}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui Tomokage|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} in [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] and the [[:en:Tenmongata|Bakufu Tenmonkata]] in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦注|1=rekichū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514953}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the [[:en:Solar calendar|Solar calendar]].

Prominent figures associated with the position include {{ill|Ōharu Manomaro|ja|大春日真野麻呂|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōharu Manomaro|1=Ōharu Manomaro|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q27920625}}, who advocated for adopting the [[:en:Goki calendar|Goki Calendar]] and [[:en:Xuanming calendar|Senmyō Calendar]] during Emperor {{ill|Seiwa|ja|Emperor Seiwa|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiwa|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'s reign, and [[:en:Kibi no Makibi|Kibi no Makibi]], credited with introducing the [[:en:Taien calendar|Dai'en Calendar]] to Japan. The 10th-century scholar {{ill|Kamo no Tadayuki|ja|賀茂忠行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo no Tadayuki|qq=}} and his son, [[:en:Kamo no Yasunori|Kamo no Yasunori]], were notable successors. After Yasunori's death, his descendants retained the ''rekidō'' lineage, while his student [[:en:Abe no Seimei|Abe no Seimei]]'s family carried on the {{ill|天文道|ja|天文道|1=Tenmondō (astrology)|lt=Tenmondō|qq= (astrology)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/天文道|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmondō (astrology)|qq=}} tradition.

Private possession of calendrical texts was strictly regulated under the {{ill|雑令|ja|雑令|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/雑令|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, particularly the ''Hisho Genjōryō,'' which inhibited the cultivation of external talent. This restriction proved significant during periods of political upheaval, such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|ja|Taira no Masakado|1=Taira no Masakado|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Masakado|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Masakado|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'s attempt to establish a rival court and the {{ill|Southern Court (Japan)|ja|南朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Southern Court (Japan)|1=Southern Dynasties|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1206988}} during the [[:en:Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|Nanboku-chō period]], neither of which could appoint a ''Reki Hakase'' or produce official calendars for their respective eras.

When the main line of the Kamo family went extinct, the {{ill|Kōtokui Family|lt=Kōtokui Family|lt=Kōtokui clan|ja|幸徳井家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui clan|qq=}}, a cadet branch, assumed the position. {{ill|Kōtokui Tomokage|ja|幸徳井友景|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui Tomokage|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a prominent figure, passed the office to his grandson {{ill|Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja|幸徳井友傳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtokui Tomotsuna|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Over time, the family's influence waned as the {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} in [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] and the [[:en:Tenmongata|Bakufu Tenmonkata]] in calendrical studies gradually overshadowed their role. Eventually, the Kōtokui family focused on {{ill|暦注|ja|暦注|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/暦注|1=rekichū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514953}} annotation alone. Following the abolition of the Onmyōryō during the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]], the position of ''Reki Hakase'' was discontinued, and its functions ceased with the adoption of the [[:en:Solar calendar|Solar calendar]].
